narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were your undergraduate GPA, your first-year law school grades, and your third-year law school grades. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. At 3.10 it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted, signaling weaker academic preparation for the rigors of the bar exam. Your first-year law school performance ranked second in importance and also pulled the outcome toward failure; you placed in the fifth decile compared with an average of sixth decile among accepted students. These two early indicators outweighed the one positive signal in your profile: your third-year grades ranked third in importance and actually worked in your favor by landing in the seventh decile, better than the 5.79 average of accepted students.

Taken together, the model concluded that your earlier academic record created too high a risk of bar exam failure. To improve your chances on a future application, focus on strengthening any remaining coursework, consider targeted bar-prep programs that address foundational gaps, and retake the LSAT if you can raise your score meaningfully above 37. Reapply once you have clearer evidence of stronger readiness. (248 words)
